title: The sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:13–28)
hook: he eats with sinners and says rest serves people, not the reverse

segments.voice: Yesterday, sins first: a man through a roof, forgiven before he walked. Your line was the deeper healing first. What did you find underneath? Day one hundred ninety-eight.

A day off, and the laptop is open on the couch. Chores get done so the day counts for something. "I'm resting," said in a tone that sounds like an apology. Rest can start to feel like a reward nobody has quite earned. In today's reading, Jesus gets into two arguments. One is about who he eats dinner with. The other is about a day of rest, and what it's for. And he settles it with one sentence. Today's word: sabbath.
screen: `A DAY OFF, FULL OF GUILT.` → `TWO ARGUMENTS.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETTLES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the dinner. Jesus walks past a tax collector named Levi, sitting at his booth, and says follow me, and Levi does. Mark sets tax collectors right beside sinners, which tells you how people saw them. Then Jesus eats at Levi's house with a crowd of tax collectors and sinners, and people object. He answers in the Douay-Rheims: "They that are well have no need of a physician, but they that are sick." Second, the word. Sabbath is the Hebrew shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease. In Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and the commandments tell Israel to keep it holy, and to let everyone rest: children, servants, foreigners, even the animals. Third, the argument. On a sabbath, Jesus's disciples pluck heads of grain as they walk through a field. Some Pharisees object that this is work. What counts as work was a real question in Jewish teaching, asked seriously. Jesus answers with a story about David, who ate the holy bread when his men were hungry. And then the sentence: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift for people, not a burden laid on them. Jewish teachers said something very close: a later rabbinic teaching puts it as the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. Fourth, what Catholics do with it. Christians came to gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and Catholics keep it as the Lord's Day: Mass, and rest from needless work.
screen: `LEVI AND A TABLE OF SINNERS.` · `SHABBAT: TO STOP.` · `GRAIN PLUCKED ON THE SABBATH.` · `REST IS A GIFT, NOT A BURDEN.` · then, large: `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a real rest, starting now. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, you're not improving yourself or getting anything done. You're stopping, which is what sabbath means. If a to-do list shows up in your head, let it go past. Let your shoulders drop, and your jaw. If you pray, you can receive this rest as a gift from God. If you don't, just receive it. The bell holds the time.
Sabbath. From the Hebrew shabbat, to stop: the day of rest, which Jesus says was made for people. Today's word.
Your line: rest is for you. Today, take one real rest, even fifteen minutes, with no guilt and no phone, and don't apologize for it. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day by attending Mass and resting from unnecessary work, and the Church teaches that Sunday rest is meant for family, prayer and care for others.

original.note: Hebrew: sabbath, from a root meaning to stop or cease.

trapdoor: what you thought: a day with lots of rules.
what it means: a gift of rest made for people, not a burden people exist to carry.
what a scholar hears: shabbat, from shavat, to cease; a close rabbinic parallel in the Mekhilta on Exodus 31:14.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 2:17 and 2:27 given from memory; confirm.
Rabbinic parallel (Mekhilta on Exodus 31:14; also Talmud Yoma 85b) paraphrased; confirm, and confirm 'later' is the right framing of its date.
Pharisees portrayed as asking a serious question within Jewish debate about sabbath work; a Keeper and a Jewish reader should check the balance.
The fasting question (2:18–22) is skipped for time.
Tax collectors 'worked for the occupiers': in Galilee, toll collectors served Herod Antipas under Roman rule; simplified.

Editor review (days 189–206): hook rewritten so it no longer asks 'have you ever' and tells the listener 'a lot of us' feel guilty; cut 'widely seen as traitors and cheats' and 'one of the great gifts of Judaism to the world' (unsourced, and praise-by-ranking); 'Christians moved their holy day' reworded so Sunday isn't framed as replacing the sabbath.
